newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - March 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - March 20.

text.p: Papua New Guinea appears set to dump its A$35 million (NZ$40 million) mercenaries contract, after a protest rally in Port Moresby on Wednesday led to riots and looting. Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan confirmed on Wednesday night that six of the 40 "military advisers" being held at army headquarters at Murray Barracks had left the country on Wednesday. Page 1.

An alleged assault by Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters on National MP John Banks was not a one-off incident, Alliance leader Jim Anderton told Parliament's privileges committee last night. Anderton was the only person to give evidence to the committee hearing his complaint that Peters assaulted Banks in a late-night altercation outside the debating chambers on March 5. Page 1.

Reserve Bank governor Don Brash says there would be merit in looking at a capital gains tax on property to stop inflationary speculation, but his idea has been quickly knocked down by government. Speaking to parliament's finance and expenditure select committee on Wednesday, Brash suggested a review of a capital gains tax on property to dampen property speculation and the resulting inflationary effects. Page 2.

New work-test measures that penalised beneficiaries for turning down jobs would apply to job-seekers with professional qualifications who refused a fruit-picking job considered suitable for them, a spokeswoman for Employment Minister Peter McCardle said on Wednesday. From April 1 beneficiaries who turn down suitable jobs, fail to turn up for a job interview or do not take part in other job-seeking activities will have their benefits cut. Page 2.

Maori Affairs Tau Henare received affidavits from three people formerly associated with the Aotearoa Television Network, but dodged questions in Parliament on Wednesday on whether he passed the documents to the Serious Fraud Office or to police. Page 2

The Cook Islands government debt to the Government Superannuation Fund had grown to about $7 million despite some repayments, fund acting chief executive Mel Smith said on Wednesday. He told Parliament's finance and expenditure select committee that he had consulted solicitor-general John McGrath about what options were available to "pursue the indebtedness". Page 2.

NZ First deputy leader Tau Henare and president Doug Woolerton have been served writs by former party colleagues who have been seeking a court review of the party's list selection process. Rix Widerstrom, who was spokesman for leader Winston Peters till a bitter falling-out last year, confirmed on Wednesday that he and a process server had served the writ on Henare at Wellington airport after a five-hour stakeout at parliament last Thursday. Page 2.

Qantas' $425.6 million sale of its 19.4 percent Air New Zealand shareholding was no surprise to analysts, who said the stake had outlived its strategic use. Qantas had sold its Air New Zealand stake for a capital gain before tax of A$99 million (NZ$113 million), chief executive James Strong said on Wednesday. The sale followed an unsolicited offer from broker ANZ Securities and had been made to institutions around the world. Qantas had listed the investment at A$267 million in its half-yearly result. Page 14.

Telecom is rated a stock to buy at $6.38 by sharebroker J B Were and Son. The recommendation compares with Salomon Brothers, which rated the stock a buy at $6.95 in a February 24 report. J.B. Were says in its March newsletter that the weakness in the Telecom share price through the share buyback period has presented an opportunity for individual investors to buy them. Page 14.

ECNZ continues to offer high-voltage input for the government's coffers, paying out $239 million in dividends in the half-year to December 31 after making a profit of $163 million. The $239 million comprised a special dividend of $158 million, paid after a revaluation of ECNZ's assets, and an ordinary dividend of $81 million, the state-owned enterprise said in the interim result announcement. Page 14.

Monetary conditions, the mix of interest rates and the level of the dollar had eased "toward" those the Reserve Bank was seeking, governor Don Brash said on Wednesday. Speaking to the government's finance and expenditure select committee at Parliament, Brash said the dollar was still "somewhat overvalued". His comments helped shave more than 20 points off the currency to leave the dollar at 69.13 U.S. cents last night, even though Brash has said this many times before. Page 14.

Power NZ has dropped court proceedings for $500,000 in exemplary damages issued against the New Zealand Stock Exchange and the Market Surveillance Panel last August. The Takapuna-based power firm filed the proceedings because it believed the panel was taking sides with rival power firm Mercury Energy which is locked in a batter for control of Power NZ. Page 14.

Bank of New Zealand has joined a growing list of financial institutions offering investors the advantages of the present tax environment with a passively managed index-tracking retail investment fund. The new trust will invest in shares that comprise the BNZ 25 Equity Index (the BNZ 25). The bank introduced its wholesale BNZ 25 Equity Index Fund (a superannuation fund for wholesale-institutional investors) earlier this month and it too invests in shares that comprise the BNZ 25. Page 14.
